insights.title: The question has moved from what GenAI can do to who can run it in production
insights.summary: Buyers no longer ask what is possible. They ask which providers can turn pilots into governed systems inside core workflows, and why their last pilots did not get there.
insights.detail: The AIM vendor study frames the 2026 market around a single buyer question: which providers can take a pilot all the way to a governed production system that lives inside day-to-day business processes. IDC's buyer survey shows the same shift from the demand side, describing agentic AI as an operational dependency rather than an experiment. When pilots fail, the cause is rarely the model. It is the data, operations, governance or organisation around it. Deloitte's 2026 report reaches the same conclusion from a 3,235-leader survey, and BCG shows the question now has an owner: 72% of CEOs call themselves the main AI decision-maker.

insights.title: Agentic AI is mainstream in intent but not yet in scaled production
insights.summary: Four in five enterprises are investing in or have deployed agentic AI, yet only a minority run several agents in production, and vendors confirm scaled agentic work is still a small share of engagements.
insights.detail: IDC finds 80 percent of large enterprises investing in or already deploying agentic AI. But the share with several agents in production ranges from 20 percent among the least mature to 59 percent among Leaders, and roughly half of the two lower tiers are still in the investing stage. AIM's vendor view agrees: agentic AI has become an active delivery priority and multi-agent platforms are launching, but agentic work that has actually reached scaled production is still a thin slice of what vendors deliver, and many of the agent references are aspirations rather than live systems. Later sources confirm the gap between intent and scaled production: Deloitte's respondents expected agent use to triple in two years, McKinsey found about one in five scaling agents in mid-2026, and Menlo and a16z found true agentic architectures in production at 13% to 16%.

insights.title: Agentic AI is the top driver of demand for real-time data
insights.summary: Advances in agentic AI are the most cited reason enterprises need faster data, ahead of security, cost and regulation.
insights.detail: In IDC's survey, 43 percent name advances in agentic AI capability as a significant driver of increased need for real-time data. Security and AI trust requirements follow at 40 percent, cost and scalability at 38, regulatory pressure at 35 and industry disruption at 29. The reading is that agents, which must sense and act on current state, are resetting expectations for data freshness. Note that the survey sponsor sells a real-time data platform.

insights.title: Capability breadth is commoditised; differentiation is now operational
insights.summary: Nearly every provider tells the same six-stage lifecycle story. What separates them is whether they can show live production systems, how deep their accelerators go, how much domain knowledge is built in, and whether their operations hold up over time.
insights.detail: AIM observes that vendors have converged on an identical end-to-end story: advisory at the front, then data groundwork, model work, application build, operations and an ongoing managed service. Because everyone claims the full lifecycle, breadth no longer differentiates. Buyers are shifting procurement scrutiny from what a vendor can build to what it has operated. Vendors that list dozens of POCs without production evidence are increasingly exposed.

insights.title: Most pilots fail and most vendors convert fewer than half
insights.summary: Industry pilot failure is reported above 70 percent, and most service providers convert only 25 to 45 percent of proofs of concept into production.
insights.detail: AIM describes the POC-to-production gap as the market's defining fault line and the primary delivery bottleneck. The small set of providers that beat the typical range share three traits: methods aimed at the human reasons projects stall (trust, skills, resistance to new ways of working); development steered by continuous evaluation, with automated quality gates throughout the build; and named production systems with quantified outcomes. Higher performers also front-load value-case validation and structured discovery, surfacing data, governance and organisational constraints before build begins. MIT NANDA's interview sample reports about 5% of custom task-specific tools reaching sustained impact within six months, and Deloitte finds only a quarter of firms with 40% or more of experiments in production. The failure rate depends on what is counted, but every source that measures it finds most pilots do not make it.

insights.title: Data quality is the number one problem from both the buyer and the vendor side
insights.summary: Two independent methods converge: IDC's buyers rank data quality and consistency as their top technical challenge, and AIM's vendors call data readiness the most cited challenge and the root cause of most production failures.
insights.detail: In the IDC survey, 46 percent cite data quality and consistency as a top technical challenge for the next 12 to 18 months, and it leads even among the most mature organisations. AIM finds that enterprise data is scattered across systems, formatted every which way, thinly documented and missing the context a language model needs, and that these problems surface only when moving from sanitised pilot samples to real production data. The gap between data that exists and data that is RAG-ready is the single largest technical friction point. Effective providers front-load data readiness assessment and treat the data groundwork as something to finish first, not something to run alongside the build. KPMG's large US firms rank data readiness the top agent barrier at 58%, and NANDA's users describe the same problem as tools that require too much context and do not learn.

insights.title: The hard part of agents is connecting them to data, not building them
insights.summary: Connecting agents to real-time enterprise data and managing them across frameworks tie as the top barriers to scaling agents. Ease of building agents ranks last.
insights.detail: IDC asked which issues are top barriers to scaling AI agents. Connecting agents to real-time enterprise data and managing agents across different frameworks each score 40 percent, followed by monitoring performance and accuracy at 37, getting agents to work together at 35, human-in-the-loop oversight at 33 and LLM cost concerns at 28. Ease of building agents is cited by only 26 percent. The picture is that tooling for building agents has matured faster than the plumbing, governance and observability needed to run many of them on live enterprise context. KPMG's mid-2026 pulse confirms it from a US sample: data readiness leads the barriers at 58% while agentic complexity and technical skills trail.

insights.title: The production gap is organisational more than technical
insights.summary: Loss of executive sponsorship, legal intervention, late compliance objections and user resistance cause more project failures than model performance.
insights.detail: AIM ranks the POC-to-production gap as the highest-impact challenge because it gates all downstream value, and states that the primary barrier is organisational readiness rather than technical capability: governance gaps, talent shortages, change-management failure and late-stage compliance objections. IDC's barrier list points the same way, with framework management, monitoring, team coordination and human oversight all ranking above building the agent itself. Vendors reporting better conversion embed production planning from engagement start instead of leaving it to the deployment stage. Deloitte's diagnosis of the pilot trap lists integration, security review, compliance and monitoring as the production requirements pilots avoid, and Microsoft's factor analysis attributes twice as much reported AI impact to organisational conditions as to individual ones.

insights.title: Hallucination erodes trust most, and it gets worse in production
insights.summary: Edge cases and domain nuance expose model weaknesses that controlled pilots mask. Responses converge on RAG-first design, citation enforcement, confidence scoring and human review.
insights.detail: AIM names hallucination and output reliability as the problem that does the most damage to buyer confidence and keeps GenAI out of regulated processes. Vendor responses converge on retrieval-grounded architectures, mandatory citations, confidence scores that route low-confidence answers to people, and a person checking the answer before it is used. A smaller group has gone further with continuous evaluation against ground-truth benchmarks as a standing production safeguard rather than one-time testing. Several vendors add critic or validator agents and deterministic rule layers on top of LLM reasoning for audit-sensitive workflows.

insights.title: Adoption, not technology, is the primary ROI risk and it is under-invested
insights.summary: Organisations spend heavily on AI technology and little on how people interact with and trust it. Vendors that treat adoption failure as the main risk produce more durable deployments.
insights.detail: AIM finds change management and adoption design broadly under-invested across the market. Too few vendors recognise that a system that works and a system people actually use are two different achievements. Effective responses put GenAI inside the tools and processes people already use instead of standing up a separate system, train each role for its own tasks, and introduce human oversight in stages so that trust grows with experience. One vendor in the study reports that redesigning outputs and interaction around behavioural insight raised adoption by 70 to 80 percent in an insurance deployment whose model was already technically sound. Three later sources agree: Deloitte finds daily use flat despite wider access and skills the top barrier, Microsoft finds organisational culture the strongest predictor of AI impact, and BCG's Trailblazer CEOs devote about 60% of AI budget to upskilling.

insights.title: Costs escalate sharply from pilot to production, though buyers rank cost below other barriers
insights.summary: Pilot token costs in the hundreds of dollars can become tens of thousands at production volume. Vendors treat cost as a design-time architectural decision; buyers rank LLM cost sixth of seven agent-scaling barriers.
insights.detail: AIM places cost management and economic viability among the top five delivery challenges and lists the standard mitigations: sending each request to the cheapest model that can handle it, caching, shortening prompts and watching spend as it happens, all settled at design time rather than after deployment. Several providers now productise cost control as gateways, FinOps dashboards or tiered model architectures that send high-volume tasks to small models. On the buyer side, IDC finds LLM cost concern cited by 28 percent as a top barrier, well behind data connectivity. A plausible reading is that vendors feel the cost pressure first, or that many buyers have not yet reached production-scale token bills. By mid-2026 the cost pressure had become measurable: McKinsey finds 20% of organisations limiting AI use on operating cost and KPMG finds only 26% with full cost visibility.

insights.title: GenAI, agents and classical ML are converging into integrated operational systems
insights.summary: Early GenAI was additive: RAG on data platforms, chatbots on portals. The emerging pattern is agents using LLMs as reasoning engines over tools, data and traditional models, with multi-agent orchestration as the design pattern for complex automation.
insights.detail: AIM calls this convergence the most consequential architectural shift in the market. Agents break a task into steps, call tools, check their own results and set off follow-on actions in other enterprise systems. For complex workflow automation the pattern gaining ground is several specialised agents coordinated together, though production examples are still a minority. Some providers explicitly fuse language models with statistical models, using the LLM as a reasoning and orchestration layer over forecasting or optimisation models to gain adaptability and explainability.

insights.title: RAG is table stakes; the edge is in retrieval quality, knowledge graphs and agentic RAG
insights.summary: Basic retrieval-augmented generation no longer differentiates. Differences show up in how documents are split for a given domain, whether retrieval quality is measured at scale, whether a knowledge graph backs the retrieval, and whether agents can drive it.
insights.detail: AIM finds that every vendor offers RAG and that enterprise knowledge retrieval is the dominant workload today. The strongest implementations span dozens of catalogues, hundreds of schemas and multiple languages within a unified reasoning platform, and they measure retrieval quality continuously. Knowledge graphs, ontology layers and semantic context layers appear across many vendor profiles as the means to ground agents and reduce hallucination. The next step is retrieval run by agents, which decide on the fly what to look up, how to reason over it and what to do next. Menlo's production data confirm it: prompt design and RAG account for over 70% of enterprise customisation approaches, with fine-tuning at 12% and tool calling at 6%.

insights.title: Knowledge retrieval dominates, content generation is shrinking, autonomous execution is growing fastest
insights.summary: The mix of GenAI work is shifting from generate-text use cases toward data-grounded retrieval and multi-step agents.
insights.detail: AIM groups vendor work into five workloads. Enterprise knowledge retrieval over internal documents and data is where most production deployments sit and the pattern enterprises adopt first. Content generation, where most organisations started, is a declining share as novelty fades. The fastest growth is in agents that carry out multi-step tasks on their own, and vendors with their own agent platforms report it approaching or exceeding half their portfolio, though the label is applied loosely by some. Domain model adaptation and multimodal processing remain selective, used where accuracy or cross-format reasoning is critical.

insights.title: The services market is splitting three ways: domain depth, owned platforms and operating maturity
insights.summary: Domain specialists with encoded regulatory and workflow knowledge, and platform-led vendors with individually named components, are building positions that generic providers cannot easily copy.
insights.detail: AIM describes three fault lines. Vendors whose prebuilt solutions carry an industry's workflows, its regulations and ready-made compliance patterns hold defensible positions. Platform-led vendors whose accelerators have specific names and specific engineering jobs show materially higher productisation maturity than those with generic capability labels. Operational maturity in LLMOps and governance is the third axis. The analyst test for an accelerator: if its description would fit any vendor, it confers little advantage.

insights.title: Accelerator counts are high, but integrated platforms are still early
insights.summary: Every vendor discloses five to ten proprietary accelerators. Most are point solutions, and full platform adoption is a small share of engagements even at the strongest vendors.
insights.detail: AIM notes that vendors list many accelerators, but few have yet pulled them together into a platform that clients adopt whole. Platform adoption rates sit in the early percentages of total engagements and multi-cloud support for flagship platforms is often still on the roadmap. One Leader reports component-level adoption in 70 to 80 percent of engagements but full platform deployment in only 10 to 15 percent. Buyers are advised to ask which accelerators have run in production for clients versus internal tools repackaged as client-ready.

insights.title: LLMOps and governance are where production viability is decided
insights.summary: Vendors that treat operations as a managed discipline with reliability engineering and cost controls, and buyers that treat governance as an accelerator, are the ones getting to scale.
insights.detail: AIM identifies LLMOps and governance as the operational layer that determines whether systems survive contact with production, and finds the strongest vendors run it with SRE discipline and FinOps controls rather than as a tooling exercise. IDC's recommendations to buyers include reframing governance as an accelerator rather than a brake, noting it is already a top investment priority; security and AI trust requirements are the second-ranked driver of real-time data demand. Six practice areas recur across vendors: cost and compute, token efficiency, monitoring, governance and risk, security and compliance, and value tracking. Deloitte and KPMG add the agent-era version: one in five has mature agent governance and half rely on output-level rather than action-level human review.

insights.title: Leaders differ from the rest in execution, not belief
insights.summary: Three quarters or more of every maturity tier agree agents need live data, yet only Leaders have actually deployed real-time data across workflows and consolidated their platforms.
insights.detail: Across IDC's charts, belief statements score 75 percent or higher in every tier. Execution measures diverge sharply: real-time data across all workflows rises from 7 percent among Emerging organisations to 76 percent among Leaders, a single unified platform from 8 to 71 percent, and automating half or more of real-time processes from 23 to 91 percent. IDC summarises it as belief being universal while execution is not. McKinsey's high performers and Microsoft's Frontier Professionals show the same pattern: the gap to everyone else is in practices such as workflow redesign, quality standards and impact measurement, not in belief.

insights.title: A unified data platform is the clearest marker of a leader; tool sprawl is the enemy
insights.summary: Seven in ten Leaders run a single unified real-time data platform versus fewer than one in ten Emerging organisations. Even so, only a third of Leaders report their technologies fully integrated.
insights.detail: IDC calls the dividing line architectural. Leaders consolidate onto unified, integrated platforms while the majority juggle many loosely connected tools they acknowledge need fixing. Tool sprawl and platform complexity is a top-five technical challenge at 37 percent, alongside legacy systems and technical debt at 38. Full integration remains rare everywhere: 36 percent of Leaders and 10 percent of Emerging organisations. Consolidation is IDC's second of five recommendations.

insights.title: Maturity pays: Leaders deliver outcomes on more than three times as many AI projects
insights.summary: 89 percent of Leaders deliver measurable outcomes on at least half their AI projects, against 26 percent of Emerging organisations. Agentic success rates roughly double across the tiers.
insights.detail: IDC's outcome measures climb steadily with maturity. The share delivering measurable outcomes on half or more of AI projects runs 26, 53, 64 and 89 percent across the four tiers. The average share of agentic projects with outcomes runs 34, 45, 54 and 67 percent, moving in step with the share of organisations running several agents in production. Reading the tiers as road-map stages, deployment and success rise together. Because the maturity score itself includes outcomes as an input, part of this relationship is definitional.

insights.title: Neither company size nor industry buys maturity
insights.summary: Real-time data maturity and AI success are flat from 500-employee firms to those with 10,000 or more, and industry gaps are modest compared with the gaps between maturity tiers.
insights.detail: IDC's maturity scores sit between 50 and 53 across all company-size bands and AI success between 46 and 51 percent. By industry, healthcare, education and software lead modestly on both measures while retail trails, but the spread is far smaller than the tier spread. IDC's conclusion is that maturity is earned through operating practices, not headcount. AIM independently notes that delivery challenges are remarkably uniform across vendor size, domain and maturity, suggesting they are industry-wide problems.

insights.title: As organisations mature, AI and data talent moves into the business
insights.summary: Leaders are more likely to embed real-time data talent in the business teams that use it, and service providers are adding forward-deployed engineers and domain expert benches for the same reason.
insights.detail: IDC finds talent embedded in business teams rising from 21 percent of Emerging organisations to 34 percent of Leaders, while distributed and loosely coordinated talent falls from 60 to 37 percent. On the supply side, AIM describes forward-deployed or embedded AI engineers who work inside client environments to bridge business and technical teams and improve conversion, and two models for domain expertise: SMEs drawn from a shared pool as needed, or a large standing bench of specialists who validate outputs and run quality checks. Even among Leaders, embedded talent is still only about one in three.

insights.title: Optimism and hype fatigue coexist
insights.summary: Four in five enterprise leaders say agentic AI is changing how they work, and seven in ten say it is overhyped. Vendors list unrealistic expectations as a recurring delivery problem.
insights.detail: IDC's respondents agree at 80 percent that agentic AI is changing the way they work and at 79 percent that it is making the world better, while 71 percent agree it is overhyped. The two views are held simultaneously. AIM's vendor study lists hype-inflated expectations from stakeholders among the challenges vendors most often report. The practical implication is that expectation-setting and value-case discipline are part of delivery, not just sales. Public opinion mirrors it: global optimism rose to 59% in 2025 while 52% remain nervous, and BCG's CEOs report easing concerns alongside rising investment.

insights.title: Real-time data investments are meeting expectations almost everywhere
insights.summary: About nine in ten organisations say their real-time data investments met or exceeded expectations, rising to 97 or 98 percent among Leaders.
insights.detail: IDC reports business outcomes met or exceeded at 85, 93, 97 and 97 percent across the four tiers and performance metrics at 87, 94, 97 and 98 percent. Satisfaction is high in every tier and increases with maturity. Given the sponsor's interest in this finding and the self-reported nature of the measure, it is best read as a sentiment indicator.

insights.title: The near-term agenda: data quality first, then GenAI and agentic support
insights.summary: Improving data and analytics quality is the top strategic objective for the next 12 to 18 months, followed closely by supporting GenAI and agentic use cases.
insights.detail: IDC's respondents rank improving data and analytics quality first at 33 percent. Supporting GenAI and agentic AI use cases and improving analytics efficiency tie at 27 percent, with process automation, app-to-app integration and reducing time from data to decision at 26 percent each. The ordering matches the challenge data: fix the data, then build on it.

insights.title: What GenAI engagements cost, by stage
insights.summary: Pilots typically run 40 to 80 thousand dollars, single-business-unit production 150 to 300 thousand, and enterprise-wide programmes 500 thousand to more than a million, with the largest reaching 2 to 4 million or more.
insights.detail: AIM's pricing benchmarks give a range and a typical cluster for each stage. Proofs of concept and pilots range from about 25 to 100 thousand dollars, with some leaders above 150 thousand. Production for a single business unit ranges 100 to 500 thousand depending on integrations and scope. Scaled, enterprise-wide programmes range from 300 thousand to more than 2 million, typically 500 thousand to a million or more. These are services fees, not platform or token costs.

insights.title: Managed services are the fastest-growing engagement model; outcome-linked pricing is rising but rare
insights.summary: Project-based work remains the entry point, run-and-operate contracts are growing fastest as production deployments increase, and only a few vendors tie fees to outcomes.
insights.detail: AIM maps six engagement models. Fixed-scope or time-and-materials projects dominate pilots and early production. Capacity-led pods are widely used as programmes expand. Run-and-operate managed services are growing fastest. Outcome-linked pricing is selective but rising in mature, KPI-driven deployments, and platform subscriptions are emerging among IP-led vendors. In the vendor profiles, only a handful describe outcome- or value-linked constructs, and a couple deliver only on fixed-scope or outcome-based terms. Vendors mature enough to align fees with results are positioned for a market moving toward accountability.

insights.title: GenAI delivery teams cluster around six to eight roles, with agentic specialists emerging
insights.summary: Data scientists and LLM engineers are the largest group, supported by data engineers, LLMOps engineers, architects, domain translators, embedded engineers, application developers and delivery governance. A distinct agentic AI architect role is appearing.
insights.detail: AIM finds team structures converge on six to eight recurring role types despite differing names. Model and application engineers consistently form the largest share, sometimes split between model-performance scientists and application-layer LLM engineers. Data engineers own pipelines, vector stores and RAG foundations. LLMOps engineers own CI/CD, serving, monitoring and cost. Domain consultants and business translators handle value mapping and adoption. Some vendors now count agentic AI architects as a separate headcount category for orchestration and tool-calling frameworks; most still fold this into the general pool.

insights.title: Domain specialisation concentrates in BFSI, healthcare and life sciences, retail and supply chain
insights.summary: Most vendors run a hybrid strategy of reusable horizontal capabilities plus a few deep verticals, and the deepest verticals are regulated or data-rich industries.
insights.detail: AIM finds hybrid strategies are the norm and that deep specialisation is most evident in banking and financial services, healthcare, retail and supply chain, the sectors where GenAI now sits inside core operations. Our count of the 28 vendor profiles supports this: financial services appears in more than 20 industry lists and healthcare or life sciences in more than 15. AIM's industry use-case matrix shows regulated industries with the longest lists of agentic use cases, such as underwriting, claims audit, regulatory dossier automation and compliance review.

insights.title: Pairing large domain expert benches with agents is a Leader strategy
insights.summary: Three of the ten Leaders run thousands of domain analysts alongside AI agents in the same workflows, using maker-checker controls and full traceability to satisfy regulated buyers.
insights.detail: Two vendors report benches of more than 6,000 domain specialists who co-execute tasks with agents, check results and apply quality controls as the work happens, and a third describes its delivery as pairing domain SMEs with AI tooling in every workflow. All three sit in the Leaders quadrant. This is the standing-bench model AIM describes, more common at vendors with managed-services or knowledge-process-outsourcing roots, and it gives them a compliance story that technology-only providers could match only by hiring comparable teams. Platform access is sometimes priced as an uplift on existing analyst fees.

insights.title: Hyperscaler and lakehouse partnerships are universal; partner tier is the differentiator
insights.summary: Nearly every vendor lists AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Databricks and Snowflake. Vendors distinguish themselves by premier or select partner status and early access to new platform capabilities.
insights.detail: Across the 28 profiles the same five platforms appear in almost every partner list, so listing them conveys little. The differentiators cited are tier and depth: top-percentile partner status, generative AI competencies, select cohorts limited to a few dozen partners globally, gold-level data-platform status with certified staff, and pre-launch access to agentic and model services that lets a vendor experiment ahead of the market. Partnerships also feed pipeline through co-sell motions.

insights.title: Synthetic personas and audiences are an emerging product category
insights.summary: At least two Leaders sell simulation platforms that test products, messaging or pricing against AI-generated customer segments before real-market research.
insights.detail: One vendor reports a persona simulation platform with a stated correlation above 95 percent to real behaviour, used for product testing, pricing and UX validation. Another reports synthetic customer cohorts for concept and message testing deployed in production for consumer goods and technology clients, with one launch cycle cut from nine months to two or three. AIM's service taxonomy lists synthetic audiences and virtual personas under application development, indicating the category has become a recognised offering.

insights.title: Disclosed conversion rates are selectively reported
insights.summary: The few vendors that publish a pilot-to-production figure report 60 percent or more, well above the 25 to 45 percent AIM says is typical. Read undisclosed as probably typical.
insights.detail: Three vendors state a conversion rate: 60 percent or more, 70 percent, and 80 percent or more. Many others describe their rate as high or above industry average without a number. Since AIM characterises most vendors as converting 25 to 45 percent, the disclosed figures are best read as the top of the distribution rather than representative. All are vendor-claimed and unaudited by the publisher. Buyers can treat a vendor's willingness to state and evidence a number as a signal in itself.

insights.title: The 2026 PeMa Quadrant: ten Leaders, and reach and maturity do not always go together
insights.summary: Ten of 28 vendors are Leaders. The highest-reach vendor and the highest-maturity vendor are different firms, and several highly mature vendors sit outside the Leaders quadrant on reach alone.
insights.detail: AIM places 10 vendors in Leaders, 9 in Seasoned Vendors, 3 in Growth Vendors and 6 in Challengers. Tiger Analytics leads on Penetration at 0.90 and Blend360 on Maturity at 0.95. The Seasoned Vendors quadrant contains firms whose maturity scores rival the Leaders but whose market reach lags, for example a vendor ranked seventh on maturity but fifteenth on penetration. Growth Vendors show the reverse pattern. Because participation is voluntary, the quadrant covers the 28 firms that took part, not the whole market.

insights.title: Five things real-time data leaders do differently
insights.summary: Treat real-time data as core AI infrastructure, consolidate onto one platform, use governance as an accelerator, connect agents to live enterprise context, and invest ahead of the curve.
insights.detail: IDC closes with five priorities that separate leading organisations. First, treat real-time, event-driven data as core AI infrastructure rather than an analytics afterthought. Second, consolidate fragmented tooling onto a unified, integrated platform, the clearest marker of a leader. Third, reframe governance as an accelerator rather than a brake. Fourth, connect agents to real-time enterprise context, since lack of context is the top barrier to production. Fifth, invest ahead of the curve: IDC states that 94 to 97 percent plan to increase real-time data and agentic investment, and the two rise together.

insights.title: How to test a GenAI service provider: ask what they have operated, not what they can build
insights.summary: Probe which accelerators run in production for clients, ask for named deployments with quantified outcomes, and ask how agent behaviour is evaluated and governed.
insights.detail: Drawing on AIM's analyst guidance across the report, three tests recur. On accelerators, ask which have been deployed in production client engagements versus internal tools repackaged as client-ready. On agentic claims, the credible vendors can explain how their agents are actually built, point to live production deployments and say how agent behaviour is tested and controlled; others label any multi-step flow as agentic. On challenges, the gap is widening between vendors that have engineered solutions to the known problems and those that merely name them, and buyers are learning to test for it earlier in procurement. AIM also reminds readers its report is one input and not a recommendation.

insights.title: Outlook: the next phase rewards proven, repeated, scaled operation
insights.summary: The vendors that last will be those with proven production deployments, real platforms, industry specialisation and the operating machinery to run AI at scale. Investment is set to keep rising on both the real-time data and agentic fronts.
insights.detail: AIM expects the market's next phase to reward proof over promise: not the fullest description of the lifecycle, but repeated evidence of having run it at scale. IDC finds near-universal intent to increase spending on real-time data and agentic AI, with the two rising together, while the near-term agenda puts data quality first. Taken together, the sources point to a market where the constraint is operational: data foundations, governance, adoption and cost discipline determine who converts intent into outcomes.

insights.title: How to read these two sources
insights.summary: One is a voluntary vendor study with unaudited self-reported data; the other is a vendor-sponsored buyer survey whose maturity score includes the outcomes it then correlates with. Both are useful, with those caveats.
insights.detail: The AIM study covers 28 vendors that chose to participate, scored from questionnaires, briefings and secondary research; vendor-submitted data is not independently audited and the publisher states it is not a recommendation. The IDC survey of 623 large-enterprise decision-makers is sponsored by a real-time data platform vendor, its framing matches the sponsor's interest, and its composite maturity score includes real-time deployment and outcomes as inputs, so correlations between maturity and those measures are partly built in. Our meta-analysis restates both in our own words, cites every figure, and gives more weight to findings where the two independent methods agree.

insights.title: Six practice areas for running GenAI at scale
insights.summary: Vendors converge on cost and compute optimisation, token efficiency, monitoring and LLMOps, governance and risk, security and compliance, and value tracking.
insights.detail: From vendor responses on how they manage large-scale implementations, AIM derives six practice areas. Cost: right-sized model selection, multi-model routing, RAG-first design, compression, caching and batching. Performance: context pruning, hybrid retrieval, structured prompts, parallel agent workflows. Monitoring: live dashboards for token use, spend, response time and accuracy, plus drift and hallucination detection, controlled releases, end-to-end observability. Governance: responsible-AI guardrails, human review for critical decisions, version control, audit trails. Security: access control, PII masking, private deployment, compliance standards. Value: KPI tracking, reusable assets, continuous optimisation.

insights.title: Security and trust are the second-biggest driver of real-time data demand
insights.summary: Security and AI trust requirements rank second among drivers of real-time data need and governance is a top-five technical challenge, which is why IDC tells buyers to treat governance as an accelerator.
insights.detail: In the IDC survey, 40 percent cite security and AI trust requirements as a driver of increased need for real-time data, just behind agentic AI at 43. Governance, security and permissions is a top technical challenge at 39 percent. IDC's advice is to reframe governance from a brake to an accelerator, noting it is already a leading investment priority. AIM's vendor data agrees from the delivery side: guardrails, audit trails, access control and compliance alignment appear in almost every vendor profile as baseline requirements for production. BCG and Deloitte confirm privacy and security as the top concern in CEO and enterprise surveys, and BCG finds more leaders now treat agents as a security opportunity than as a threat.

insights.title: Enterprise spend on generative AI reached about $37 billion in 2025, more than tripling
insights.summary: Menlo Ventures sizes 2025 enterprise generative AI spend at about $37B, up 3.2x, split almost evenly between infrastructure and applications. Per-company budgets and capital-market data point the same way.
insights.detail: Menlo's bottom-up model excludes chips, inference hosting and AI features bundled into existing software, so it understates total AI outlay. Within its scope, model APIs took $12.5B and applications $19B, with horizontal copilots the largest single line. a16z's Global 2000 CIOs report average LLM spend of about $7M per firm in 2025, up from $2.5M actually spent in 2024 (the prose cites a $4.5M baseline that was a forecast), and average application spend of about $5.8M per firm against a planned $3.9M. Stanford's compilation of Quid data shows private AI investment of about $345B in the same year, an order of magnitude larger because it measures capital into AI companies rather than enterprise purchases. All three lenses more than doubled in 2025.

insights.title: AI budgets are still rising in 2026, but expectations for the pace moderated during the year
insights.summary: Early-2026 surveys expected AI spend to double; mid-2026 surveys show continued growth at a lower rate. Growth is not in doubt, the rate is.
insights.detail: BCG's CEOs in January 2026 expected AI investment to rise from 0.8% to 1.7% of revenue during the year, and a16z's CIOs projected 65% growth in LLM spend. By May and June, McKinsey found 61% expecting to increase AI investment but only 8% by 30% or more, and KPMG's large US firms reported projected 12-month spend flat quarter on quarter at about $200M after doubling over the prior year. Every source still shows growth, and BCG found 94% would keep investing even if 2026 returns disappointed. The time ordering matters: the two surveys fielded latest show the softest profile. Our reading is a market moving from step change to steady growth, which the 2027 editions will confirm or refute.

insights.title: Coding is generative AI's first killer use case
insights.summary: Software development is where spend, measured productivity, vendor competition and scaled agent use all concentrate. Coding tools were about $4B in 2025, five times the prior year.
insights.detail: Menlo puts coding at more than half of departmental AI spend, with code agents growing from near zero to $1.1B and half of developers using AI coding tools daily. Stanford's compilation of controlled studies records a 26% rise in pull requests for developers using an AI assistant, with juniors gaining most. McKinsey finds about a fifth of organisations scaling coding agents in mid-2026, rising to 31% at large firms, and a third have declined to buy software because coding agents let them build it. a16z's CIOs say model leadership in coding is what shifted their vendor mix, and Lightcast data in the AI Index show agentic-skill mentions in job postings rising more than a hundredfold. The pattern is consistent: verifiable, structured work with a paying developer audience adopts first.

insights.title: Startups are winning AI applications while incumbents hold infrastructure and the enterprise seat
insights.summary: AI-native startups took about 63% of application revenue in 2025, yet almost every large enterprise pays for Microsoft 365 Copilot and two thirds prefer an incumbent when one exists.
insights.detail: Menlo's revenue data show startups ahead in departmental (60%), vertical (88%) and horizontal (57%) applications but behind in infrastructure (44%), where application builders stay on established data platforms. a16z's Global 2000 survey shows the other side: 94% pay for Microsoft 365 Copilot, 74% for GitHub Copilot, and 65% prefer incumbents, citing trust, integration and easier procurement. Startups are chosen for faster innovation and deeper AI focus. MIT NANDA's interviews add that a trusted vendor is the top selection criterion and that many procurement leaders wait for an incumbent's AI feature rather than evaluate startups. The two pictures fit a market where incumbents own the broad seat licence and startups own the high-value, high-token workloads.

insights.title: Who leads enterprise LLMs depends on who is counting, but the direction of travel is shared
insights.summary: Menlo ranks Anthropic first by API usage; a16z ranks OpenAI first by production footprint among Global 2000 firms. Each firm invests in the vendor it places first. Both agree Anthropic is gaining fastest, Google is rising, open-weight models are losing share and multi-model use is the norm.
insights.detail: Menlo estimates Anthropic at 40% of enterprise LLM API usage in 2025, OpenAI 27% and Google 21%, from a US sample of 495 that includes AI-native builders and weights by application scale. a16z finds 78% of Global 2000 respondents using OpenAI in production and a 56% average wallet share, with Anthropic at 44% production use and 17% wallet share, from 100 large firms with coding startups excluded. Read together, OpenAI has the widest footprint in large incumbents' estates and Anthropic has the larger share of token-intensive coding work and the fastest growth. Both surveys show open-weight models at about a tenth of enterprise usage and falling, four in five enterprises running three or more model families, and fine-tuning giving way to prompting and routing. The site presents both estimates with their samples and conflicts of interest and does not declare a single leader.

insights.title: Buying beats building, in five sources, with one new counter-current from coding agents
insights.summary: Purchased AI use cases rose from 53% to 76% in a year, bought solutions reach production about twice as often as internal builds, and enterprises are migrating from DIY model builds to packaged applications. McKinsey adds that a third have declined a software purchase because coding agents let them build it.
insights.detail: Menlo's survey shows the purchase share jumping to 76% and bought AI converting to production at 47% against 25% for conventional software. MIT NANDA's interviews find externally sourced tools reaching deployment about 66% of the time versus 33% for internal builds, with roughly double the employee usage. a16z's CIOs report a shift toward third-party applications in every tracked use case, and AIM's providers report buyers demanding production evidence rather than bespoke builds. Deloitte's pilot-trap diagnosis explains why: production needs integration, security, compliance and monitoring that internal pilots skip. McKinsey's mid-2026 finding that 32% have forgone a purchase in favour of building with coding agents, rising to about half of high performers, is not a contradiction: enterprises buy applications and platforms and build the long tail of features they once bought. It is the first survey evidence that agentic coding is changing software budgets.

insights.title: Healthcare buys packaged vertical AI; regulated finance buys services instead
insights.summary: Healthcare took about 43% of vertical AI software spend in 2025, led by ambient scribes, while finance and insurance software markets stayed tiny even though financial services is the deepest specialisation among AI service providers.
insights.detail: Menlo's vertical spend data put healthcare at $1.5B, more than the next four verticals combined, with finance at $120M and insurance under $100M. AIM's vendor study finds BFSI in the industry lists of more than 20 of 28 providers and the deepest vertical solutions in banking, insurance and healthcare. The reconciliation is that regulated financial institutions buy custom, services-led delivery with compliance blueprints rather than packaged products, which is exactly the market AIM's providers serve, while healthcare found a packaged product (clinical documentation) with immediate, measurable relief from administrative burden. NANDA's disruption index supports the distinction: healthcare is buying AI without its clinical models being restructured yet.

insights.title: Where AI is built now matters as much as what it does: sovereignty has become a planning input
insights.summary: More than four in five large companies treat data residency and local compute as at least moderately important, three quarters weigh a vendor's country of origin, and publics trust the EU more than the US or China to regulate AI.
insights.detail: Deloitte's late-2025 survey found 83% rating data-residency and in-country compute at least moderately important to strategic planning, 66% at least moderately concerned about reliance on foreign-owned AI, 77% factoring country of origin into vendor selection and 58% building their stacks mainly with local vendors. The pressure is regional: 11% of Americas firms source most of their stack abroad against 32% in EMEA. Stanford's compilation adds the demand-side signal that a 25-country median of 53% trusts the EU to regulate AI versus 37% for the US and 27% for China, and that US trust in its own regulator is the lowest surveyed at 31%. a16z's largely US and UK sample shows the opposite motion, with four in five hosting models directly with frontier labs, which suggests geography rather than a single global trend. No other source in this project measures sovereignty directly, so the Deloitte figures stand alone on the enterprise side.

insights.title: Physical AI is in most adopters’ operations, led by Asia Pacific, but robot installations were flat in 2024
insights.summary: Deloitte finds 58% of AI-using companies already use robotics, drones or automated machinery to some extent and expects 80% within two years. Robot shipment data temper the pace: global installations were flat in 2024 and US installations fell.
insights.detail: In Deloitte's survey, Asia Pacific leads with 71% reporting at least minimal physical AI use against 56% in the Americas and EMEA, and expected use reaches 90% in Asia Pacific. Intelligent monitoring, collaborative robots and digital twins are the types expected to matter most, and cost is the top barrier because facility retrofits, integration and maintenance dwarf the AI software. The International Federation of Robotics data compiled by Stanford show 542,000 industrial robots installed in 2024, up 0.2%, with China at 54% of the world and the US down 9%; collaborative robots reached 13.6% of installations. Microsoft's telemetry adds that manufacturing firms are few in number among agent adopters but run the deepest agent estates. Physical AI is real and concentrated in Asia and in controlled environments; the two-year jump to 80% is an expectation, not a trend.

insights.title: Agent adoption figures range from single digits to more than half, and the definition explains the spread
insights.summary: Sources report agent use anywhere from 7% to 59% because they measure different things: any use, self-reported moderate use, deployment, scaling, or an architectural test of what counts as an agent.
insights.detail: On the most inclusive measure, McKinsey's surveys compiled by Stanford put organisational AI use at 88% to 89%. Self-reported agent use follows: KPMG finds 53% of large US firms with agents deployed, IDC 20% to 59% by maturity tier with several agents in production, Deloitte 23% using agentic AI at least moderately. Stage-based measures fall further: McKinsey finds about 20% scaling agents overall and 40% at $1B-plus firms, while its 2025 data put scaled agent use in single digits per function. The strictest measures are architectural: Menlo classifies 16% of enterprise deployments as true agents that plan, act, observe and adapt, and a16z finds agentic workflow automation in production at 13%. The ladder from any use to scaled, governed agents is the finding. The site places each source on it rather than quoting one number.

insights.title: One in four has moved most experiments to production; what you buy converts better than what you build
insights.summary: A quarter of Deloitte's respondents have 40% or more of AI experiments in production. Across sources, bought general tools and packaged applications convert best, vendor-run pilots sit in the middle, and bespoke internal builds convert worst.
insights.detail: Deloitte finds 25% at the 40%-in-production threshold, with 54% expecting to reach it within six months. Menlo's funnel shows purchased AI reaching production 47% of the time. AIM's providers convert 25% to 45% of proofs of concept. MIT NANDA's interview sample shows general-purpose tools implemented by 40% of organisations that investigated them, while custom or task-specific tools reached sustained impact in about 5% of cases, and external partnerships succeeded twice as often as internal builds. The ranking is consistent once the denominators are lined up, and it explains why the same market can show high failure rates and fast-growing spend at the same time.

insights.title: What the '95% of pilots fail' figure actually measures, and why it coexists with tripling spend
insights.summary: MIT NANDA's headline is the share of custom, task-specific GenAI tools reported as reaching sustained P&L impact within about six months in a 52-organisation interview sample. It is not a market-wide failure rate, and it does not contradict spend growth.
insights.detail: NANDA's funnel shows 60% of organisations investigating embedded or task-specific tools, 20% piloting and 5% reporting marked, sustained impact, judged roughly six months after the pilot; the authors call the figures directional and note that success definitions vary by organisation. The report's executive summary restates this as 95% of organisations getting zero return, which changes the unit from tools to organisations. Menlo cites the figure as the trigger of mid-2025 bubble fears and answers with $37B of enterprise spend growing 3.2x. AIM independently reports pilot failure above 70% alongside a growing services market. High per-pilot failure and rising aggregate spend are different measures and both can be true. NANDA's own general-purpose funnel converts 40 of 80, and its build-versus-buy gap of 33% against 66% is the same finding from another angle. The site quotes the 95% only with its definition and sample.

insights.title: Access to AI tools grew by half in a year; daily use did not move
insights.summary: Sanctioned access rose from under 40% to about 60% of workers, but fewer than 60% of those with access use AI daily, a ratio unchanged from the prior year. Four sources describe this activation gap from different angles.
insights.detail: Deloitte names activation rather than availability as the primary barrier to value. KPMG's mid-2026 pulse shows employee adoption of agents falling from 55% to 43% in a quarter. Microsoft's survey of 20,000 AI users finds one in ten skilled but blocked by an unready organisation and only 13% rewarded for reinvention when results do not follow. MIT NANDA and Menlo show why official tools are judged harshly: workers at more than 90% of companies use personal AI tools regularly while 40% of companies have an official subscription, and employee-paid tools push product-led spend toward 40% of application spend. Employees have a private benchmark for what good AI feels like, and enterprise deployments are measured against it. a16z's finding that Copilot's net promoter score among developers fell 48 points after they tried Cursor makes the same point.

insights.title: Individual productivity gains are broad; enterprise financial impact is concentrated and flat
insights.summary: Eight in ten people say AI improves their own productivity, but only 37% of organisations attribute any EBIT impact to it and 6% qualify as high performers, both unchanged year on year. Efficiency is delivered; revenue is still an aspiration.
insights.detail: McKinsey's 2026 survey quantifies the gap in one sample: 80% report personal productivity gains, 37% attribute EBIT impact, 6% attribute 5% or more of EBIT. Deloitte finds efficiency and productivity achieved by 66% but revenue growth by 20%, with 74% still hoping for it. a16z's CIOs report ROI on LLM spend at break-even or worse in half of cases and 44% do not measure it precisely. Stanford's compilation of McKinsey's 2025 data shows the same ordering of outcomes: innovation improved for 64%, cost for 38%, revenue growth for 33%, market share for 25%. BCG's CEOs invest regardless. Four surveys with four fieldwork windows agree that spending follows productivity belief while enterprise-level financial proof remains rare.

insights.title: Company size buys breadth of deployment, not maturity of practice
insights.summary: McKinsey finds large enterprises far ahead on scaling AI and agents; IDC and AIM find maturity and delivery challenges flat across company size. The measures differ and both hold.
insights.detail: In McKinsey's 2026 survey, 54% of respondents at $1B-plus firms report enterprise-wide scaling against 33% at smaller firms, and agent scaling reached 40% at large firms versus 22% below. Stanford's compilation of the 2025 edition shows scaled or fully scaled deployment rising from 30% in the smallest revenue band to 49% in the largest. IDC's real-time data maturity score and AI success rate barely move from 500 to 10,000-plus employees, and AIM finds the same delivery challenges at vendors of every size. Large firms have the budget and IT capacity to run more programmes further, but scaling more programmes does not raise the outcome rate per project. MIT NANDA's interviews add that top mid-market firms move from pilot to full implementation in about 90 days against nine months or more for enterprises.

insights.title: Reasoning models sped up adoption, and prompting plus retrieval remains the production norm
insights.summary: More than half of large-enterprise CIOs say reasoning models accelerated LLM adoption. In production, prompt design and RAG dominate; fine-tuning, tool calling and context engineering are still niche.
insights.detail: a16z's respondents credit reasoning models with faster time to value, less prompt engineering, better integration and higher trust from explainability, and say they have moved away from fine-tuning toward routing across models. Menlo's architecture data show prompt design at 38% and RAG at 34% of enterprise customisation approaches, with fine-tuning at 12%, tool calling and context engineering at 6% each. AIM's vendor study reached the same conclusion from the supply side: RAG is table stakes and differentiation sits in retrieval quality. Startups lead on the newer techniques, which suggests enterprises will follow as tool-calling patterns mature.

insights.title: Executives expect agents to become a majority practice within two years; mid-2026 data show a pause
insights.summary: Deloitte's respondents expected agentic AI use to rise from 23% to 74% within two years, and IDC predicts half of enterprises using agents by 2027. KPMG's quarterly data in mid-2026 show deployment flat at about half of large US firms.
insights.detail: Deloitte's late-2025 survey projected at-least-moderate agent use climbing from 23% to 74%, with extensive use from 2% to 23%. BCG's CEOs committed more than 30% of 2026 AI budgets to agents and about 90% expected agents to deliver measurable ROI during the year. McKinsey's mid-2026 survey found agent scaling jumping from 27% to 40% at large firms but flat at 22% below $1B. KPMG's Q2 2026 pulse shows deployment at 53% versus 55% a quarter earlier, with the mix shifting from scaling across functions toward orchestrating across workflows. IDC's forecast of half of enterprises by 2027 sits inside the range the self-reports already claim. The expected surge is plausible on the self-reported measures and unproven on stage-based and architectural ones.

insights.title: Most production “agents” are workflows around a model call; repeatable agent processes are rare
insights.summary: Only 16% of enterprise deployments meet an architectural definition of an agent, 13% of large enterprises run agentic workflow automation in production, and only about a quarter of the most advanced AI users report documented, repeatable agent workflows.
insights.detail: Menlo classifies 39% of enterprise deployments as fixed-sequence workflows, 26% routing-based and 18% single-shot, with multi-agent systems at 8% and single- or multi-trajectory agents at 5% and 3%. a16z's use-case data put agentic internal workflow automation in production at 13%, the lowest of six use cases. Microsoft's survey finds that even Frontier Professionals report documented agent workflows and handoffs at only 25% to 29% at team, function and organisation level, against 14% to 19% for others, and its 15x growth in active agents is from an undisclosed base. Agents are spreading, but most are not yet embedded in governed, repeatable processes, which is where the value and the risk both sit.

insights.title: Orchestration across workflows is the layer buyers and vendors are converging on
insights.summary: The share of large US firms orchestrating multiple agents across workflows doubled in one quarter, most leading service providers now sell an orchestration platform, and managing agents across frameworks is a top buyer barrier.
insights.detail: KPMG's pulse shows orchestration rising from 9% to 18% of large US firms between Q1 and Q2 2026 while scaling across functions slipped and piloting grew. AIM's vendor profiles show at least 18 of 28 providers with a named multi-agent orchestration platform. IDC's buyers rank managing agents across different frameworks joint top among scaling barriers at 40%, ahead of building agents, which ranks last. Demand and supply are moving to the same layer, and interoperability protocols such as MCP and A2A are the emerging plumbing that MIT NANDA also points to.

insights.title: Agent governance lags agent deployment everywhere except among the leaders
insights.summary: One in five companies has a mature governance model for autonomous agents, half rely on output-level rather than action-level human review, and a third are mitigating unauthorised agent actions. Autonomy is expected to roughly triple within three years.
insights.detail: Deloitte finds 21% with mature agent governance while 74% plan at least moderate agent use within two years. KPMG's preferred control, named by 52% for the second quarter running, is a person validating outputs without supervising each agent action. McKinsey provides the first direct measure of agent-action risk: 33% mitigate unauthorised or unintended action, rising to 45% among high performers. BCG's CEOs expect systems that work independently to rise from 14% to 39% and systems with decision authority from 10% to 35% within three years. Deloitte's prescription of explicit autonomy boundaries, real-time monitoring and full audit trails, and Microsoft's advice to treat agents as managed identities with permissions and lifecycle, describe the same gap. It is being closed by the leading minority first.

insights.title: Agents raise the demand for human judgment before they lower headcount
insights.summary: Half of AI users say quality control of AI output is the skill gaining most importance, 86% keep responsibility for the thinking, and buyers name human-oversight skills the second-biggest barrier to deploying agents.
insights.detail: Microsoft's survey of 20,000 AI users puts quality control of AI output (50%) and critical thinking (46%) at the top of rising skills. KPMG's buyers rank human oversight skills such as human-in-the-loop judgment and escalation at 43%, behind only data readiness. Deloitte's interviewees expect staff to spend more time watching agent volume and quality metrics and handling human-in-the-loop gates before any headcount effect. AIM's providers list human-in-the-loop patterns as the standard reliability control. Human evaluation capacity is the shared bottleneck, and it is the workforce implication executives' automation forecasts tend to skip.

insights.title: Coding agents are starting to displace software purchases
insights.summary: A third of organisations have declined to buy at least one software product or feature because coding agents let them build it in-house, rising to about half of AI high performers.
insights.detail: McKinsey's mid-2026 survey is the first to measure this. The decline-to-buy share is highest in technology (41%), healthcare (39%), professional services and energy (38%) and lowest in insurance (19%) and the public sector (17%). High performers also hit token-cost limits on coding agents three times as often as others, which shows the build option is not free. Menlo had already noted that the race between deep third-party applications and improving model capability is most intense in software development. This is a single-source measurement and an early signal; the site presents it as a trend to watch rather than an established shift.

insights.title: Demand for agentic skills exploded in job postings while chat-tool skills lost share
insights.summary: US job postings mentioning agentic AI rose more than a hundredfold in a year and RAG was among the fastest-growing skills, while the share of AI postings mentioning ChatGPT and conversational AI fell even as their absolute counts still grew.
insights.detail: Lightcast data compiled by Stanford show postings mentioning agentic AI rising from 151 to 16,541 between 2024 and 2025, AI agents from 1,310 to 15,217 and context engineering from 9 to 703, while the share of AI postings citing ChatGPT fell 35% and conversational AI 68% (their absolute counts still rose, by 160% and 28%). Scalability and workflow-management skills also grew strongly, but Stanford measures those against 2013 to 2015 rather than year on year. AI skills reached 2.6% of all US postings and above 4% in Singapore. The posting figures come from Stanford alone; the demand-side data corroborate what the supply side says it needs: AIM's providers report the shift from assistive to agentic delivery and name LLMOps and agentic design talent as scarce, and KPMG's buyers list human-oversight and cost-literacy skills as barriers.

insights.title: Data readiness tops agent barriers in two buyer surveys and a provider survey
insights.summary: Data readiness and access lead KPMG's agent barriers at 58%, connecting agents to enterprise data ties for first in IDC's at 40%, and AIM calls the gap between data that exists and data that is RAG-ready the largest technical friction. MIT NANDA's users describe the same problem as tools that do not learn or retain context.
insights.detail: Three surveys from different populations and continents agree on the top barrier. KPMG's large US firms put data readiness far ahead of skills and complexity. IDC's eight-country sample ranks connecting agents to real-time data joint first at 40%, level with managing agents across frameworks, and data quality first among technical challenges at 46%. AIM's providers name data readiness the technical root cause of most production failures. NANDA adds the user's view: about two thirds reject generic tools for core workflows because they do not learn from feedback or require too much manual context each time, and 66% of executives want systems that learn. Memory, context and data readiness are one problem seen from the user, the buyer and the vendor, and the data-platform work IDC associates with leaders is its remedy.

insights.title: AI operating cost has become a measured constraint, and the heaviest users feel it first
insights.summary: One in five organisations has limited AI use because of operating costs including tokens, only a quarter of large US firms can see those costs in full, and high performers hit cost limits on coding agents three times as often as others.
insights.detail: McKinsey's mid-2026 survey finds 20% constraining AI use on cost, fairly evenly across industries, with 18% of high performers constrained on coding agents against 6% of others. KPMG finds 26% with full cost visibility despite 66% running cost dashboards and 61% reviewing cost at approval; token budgets exist at 36%, and cost literacy is now a named skills barrier. AIM warned that token and operating costs scale from hundreds of dollars in a proof of concept to tens of thousands at production volume and should be treated as an architectural decision. Menlo invokes Jevons' paradox and McKinsey describes the same effect without naming it: unit prices fall, volumes rise faster, so AI is not becoming too cheap to meter. Cost discipline is forming as a standard practice, led by the organisations that use AI most.

insights.title: Usage incentives such as token-maxxing risk rewarding the wrong behaviour
insights.summary: Two in five large US firms would consider rewarding employees for consuming as many tokens as possible, often via leaderboards, while fewer than half of leaders agree that heavy AI users are outperforming others.
insights.detail: KPMG's Q2 2026 pulse records 41% open to token-maxxing incentives at the same time as only 47% agree that strong AI users outperform and employee resistance driven by workload is rising. KPMG's own summary warns that metrics based on usage rather than outcomes reinforce the wrong habits. Microsoft's finding that only 13% of AI users are rewarded for reinvention when results do not follow shows the opposite failure: incentives that never reward experimentation. The organisations in McKinsey's high-performer group tie AI use to performance management and measure impact with defined processes, which is the middle path the two extremes miss.

insights.title: Data privacy and security top every concern list, and the concern is turning into an investment area
insights.summary: Privacy and security is the leading AI concern in the BCG, Deloitte and KPMG surveys and among the risks McKinsey's respondents most often mitigate, but it is easing in BCG's executive survey and more leaders now see agents as a security opportunity than as a threat.
insights.detail: BCG's executives (2,360 respondents, 27% of them CEOs) rank data privacy and cybersecurity first at 53%, down 12 points from 2025, and 32% call cybersecurity the biggest opportunity of agentic AI against 9% who call it the biggest threat. Deloitte's respondents put data privacy and security at 73%, followed by compliance at 50% and governance capability and model quality at 46% each. Data security, privacy and risk is the top factor shaping strategy for 92% of KPMG's large US firms, and cybersecurity is their most common mid-size investment line at 55%. McKinsey's most-mitigated risks are inaccuracy, cyber exploitation and social engineering. IDC's buyers rank security and AI trust the second driver of real-time data demand. The concern is not going away; it has become a budget line.

insights.title: Override rules and accountability for AI decisions are still informal at many large firms
insights.summary: A third of large US firms override AI outputs case by case without formal criteria, and accountability for AI-informed decisions is split between named executives and the CEO or executive committee, with governance committees rarely in charge.
insights.detail: KPMG finds the most common override triggers are a conflict with regulatory or legal requirements (47%) and confidence or quality scores below limits (43%), but 33% have no formal criteria and only 29% use predefined risk thresholds. Accountability sits with a named C-suite executive such as the CIO, CAIO or COO at 34%, the CEO or executive committee at 32%, a business unit leader at 14% and a central AI governance committee at 10%. Deloitte's interviews surfaced organisations with no inventory of the models running in production. The picture is of governance that exists as principle and dashboard but not yet as rule. It is a single-source measurement on the override question.

insights.title: Publics are more nervous than executives, and trust in regulators is lowest in the United States
insights.summary: Global optimism about AI rose to 59% in 2025 while about half stay nervous. The US public expects AI to eliminate jobs by two to one, only 31% trust the US government to regulate AI, and every US state has more people wanting stronger federal rules than weaker ones.
insights.detail: Stanford's compilation of Ipsos, Pew and CHIP50 data is the only public-opinion evidence in this project. Sentiment is most positive in China, Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia and most nervous in Australia, the US, India and Great Britain. US experts and the public diverge sharply: 73% of experts but 23% of the public expect AI to improve how people do their jobs. A 25-country median trusts the EU (53%) more than the US (37%) or China (27%) to regulate AI. Executive surveys in this project are most confident in exactly the markets where publics are most optimistic, which suggests public sentiment is a real constraint on adoption in the West that CEO and CIO surveys do not capture.

insights.title: AI has become a CEO-owned agenda
insights.summary: Nearly three quarters of CEOs call themselves the main AI decision-maker, double the prior year, and two thirds of large US firms say their CEO actively owns AI with clear accountability. Visible senior ownership is a top high-performer practice.
insights.detail: BCG's 640 CEOs put themselves in charge at 72%, and half tie their own job stability to getting AI right by 2026. KPMG's leaders corroborate it at 67%. McKinsey finds senior leaders visibly owning AI initiatives at 65% of high performers against 31% of others, one of the widest practice gaps in its survey. Ownership and accountability are not the same thing, though: KPMG shows accountability for individual AI-informed decisions split between named executives and the CEO. AIM's observation that buyers now ask why their last pilots failed has an owner.

insights.title: Organisational conditions explain twice as much AI impact as individual effort; demographics almost none
insights.summary: Across 29 factors in a survey of 20,000 AI users, organisational AI culture, talent practices and manager support outrank every individual factor, and age, job level, function, industry and company size explain almost nothing.
insights.detail: Microsoft's random-forest analysis attributes 67% of explained variation in reported AI impact to organisational factors and 32% to individual ones, with organisational culture at the top and the strongest individual factor (AI mindset) less than half as important. Microsoft states the results are associations, not causes, and the sample excludes non-users. The finding is nonetheless the workforce-side mirror of what buyer and vendor surveys say: AIM's providers call adoption failure the main ROI risk, Deloitte finds skills the top integration barrier and 84% of firms without job redesign, and BCG's Trailblazer CEOs put about 60% of AI budget into upskilling. Manager behaviour moves the numbers: employees whose managers openly use AI, set quality standards and make room to experiment report far higher impact.

insights.title: Work has not been redesigned around AI, and redesign is the strongest single marker of leaders
insights.summary: 84% of large companies have not redesigned jobs around AI and only 16% have adopted flatter structures, yet about three quarters of McKinsey's high performers have fundamentally redesigned workflows against a quarter of others.
insights.detail: Deloitte's late-2025 survey finds most talent responses stop at education and fluency: 53% educate the workforce, 33% redesign career paths, 30% reorganise around new work patterns. McKinsey's high performers redesign workflows at about 73%, up from 55% a year earlier, versus about 25% of others, and are 3.3 times more likely to intend fundamental transformation within three years. BCG's Trailblazers are far more likely to see end-to-end transformation as their greatest agent opportunity, and IDC's Leaders have real-time data across all workflows at 76% against 7% for its Emerging tier. Microsoft's data say the same from the employee side: Frontier Professionals redesign workflows routinely and their teams discuss quality standards and share what works. The leading group is defined by operating-model change rather than tools or budget.

insights.title: Employee resistance is rising, and its cause is shifting from fear to workload
insights.summary: Employee adoption of agents at large US firms fell from 55% to 43% in one quarter while resistance rose from 5% to 20%. Concerns about skills and job security eased; resistance because AI makes work feel harder nearly doubled.
insights.detail: KPMG's Q2 2026 pulse attributes 51% of resistance to added workload or complexity, up from 28%, while concern about skills gaps fell from 76% to 57% and about job security from 67% to 55%. McKinsey finds the strain concentrated below executive level: 47% of midlevel managers and individual contributors report at least one negative effect such as pressure to take on more work or weaker critical thinking, versus 31% of executives. Microsoft's AI users say it feels safer to focus on current goals than to redesign work (45%) even though 65% fear falling behind. Executives who answer these surveys experience AI differently from the people expected to adopt it, which helps explain the flat daily-use rate Deloitte reports.

insights.title: Workforce cuts expected from AI run about double the cuts actually reported
insights.summary: Organisations that expected AI-driven headcount reductions in 2025 (32%) reported them a year later at 14%, then raised their expectation for the next year to 39%. Other executive surveys show even larger expectations; the one study of realised effects shows limited, selective cuts.
insights.detail: McKinsey's 2026 survey provides the only before-and-after check in this project, and the pattern held among the 552 respondents who answered in both years. Deloitte's respondents expect at least 10% of jobs fully automated within a year (36%) and within three years (82%), and BCG's CEOs expect more than half of roles gone or transformed by 2030 (60%). MIT NANDA's mid-2025 interviews found layoffs limited and confined to already-disrupted sectors, with reductions of 5% to 20% in customer support and administrative processing at advanced adopters, mostly in previously outsourced roles. Service operations and supply chain lead both expectations and realised cuts in McKinsey's data. The evidence supports discounting stated automation expectations heavily while watching the functions where cuts have begun.

insights.title: Entry-level workers bear the early labour cost even though they gain most in productivity studies
insights.summary: Employment of US software developers aged 22 to 25 fell close to 20% from its 2022 peak while older cohorts grew, and the same age band declined about 16% in the most AI-exposed occupations relative to the least. In controlled studies, the least experienced workers gain the most from AI.
insights.detail: Stanford's compilation of Brynjolfsson and colleagues' payroll analysis shows the decline widening from mid-2024 and holding after firm-level controls, with a matching pattern for customer service agents. The same chapter reports productivity gains of 30% to 35% for the least experienced support agents and the largest Copilot gains for junior developers. Deloitte's interviewees worry that automating data entry, reconciliation and first-line support removes the first rung of careers, and Lightcast data show employers creating at least 1.3 million AI-related roles while junior hiring falls. The productivity dividend and the hiring cut fall on the same group from different directions, which makes career pathways a design problem rather than a side effect.

insights.title: Emerging Asia and the Gulf lead on AI confidence and practice; Japan and Western Europe trail
insights.summary: CEO confidence runs from 76% in India to 44% in the UK, the share of Frontier Professionals from 39% in Vietnam to 8% in France, and public optimism from 85% in China to 42% in the US. The ranking repeats across four independent sources.
insights.detail: BCG finds CEOs in India, Greater China and Japan most confident that AI will pay off and least pressured to act, while UK and US CEOs are the reverse. Microsoft's survey of AI users finds the largest shares of advanced practitioners and the strongest leadership alignment in Vietnam, Indonesia, India and Thailand, and the lowest in France, the Netherlands, Italy and Japan. Deloitte shows Asia Pacific leading physical AI adoption, and Stanford's compilation shows the UAE and Singapore leading population diffusion, the US 24th, and publics in China and Southeast Asia far more optimistic than in the US, Canada or Western Europe. Japan is the exception worth stating: confident at CEO level in BCG, weak on workforce practice and leadership alignment in Microsoft.

insights.title: How big the leading group is depends entirely on where the bar is set
insights.summary: Sources put the share of organisations that are ahead at 1%, 6%, 15%, 16% to 19%, 20% and 34%. Practice-based definitions cluster at 15% to 20%; the extremes come from an EBIT test and from self-described ambition.
insights.detail: IDC's maturity benchmark counts 1% as optimised AI-fuelled enterprises with no method given. McKinsey's high performers, who attribute 5% or more of EBIT to AI, are 6%. BCG's Trailblazer CEOs are about 15%. Microsoft's Frontier Professionals are 16% of AI users and its Frontier zone 19%. IDC's real-time data Leaders are the top 20%. Deloitte's deep transformers are 34% because the question asks about ambition rather than practice. The consistent message is that the leading group is small and is defined by execution and operating-model change, not by size or budget. The site presents the range with each definition rather than one number.

insights.title: What the leaders do differently, across five surveys
insights.summary: The leading minority invests more of its budget in people, redesigns workflows end to end, has visible senior ownership, measures impact, manages cost, sets human-in-the-loop rules and runs a unified data platform. Every survey that profiles leaders finds a version of this list.
