insights.detail: BCG's Trailblazers put about 60% of AI budget into upskilling and about 60% into agentic AI, invest more than $50M and upskill more than half the workforce at two to three times the rate of others. McKinsey's high performers lead on transformative ambition (62% vs 17%), workflow redesign (73% vs 25%), senior leaders visibly owning AI (65% vs 31%), defined impact measurement (40% vs 20%), active cost management (41% vs 25%) and a semantic layer (35% vs 13%), and they scale agents in three times as many functions. IDC's Leaders run a single unified data platform at 71% against 8% for its Emerging tier and embed talent in the business. Microsoft's Frontier Professionals have managers who set quality standards for AI work and teams that share what works. AIM's strongest providers show the same traits from the vendor side: production evidence, evaluation-driven development and named operational practices.

insights.title: ROI is measured loosely and reported as modest
insights.summary: Large enterprises measure AI return mostly as productivity (72%) and cost savings (53%); 44% believe it is positive without measuring it precisely; half report break-even or worse on LLM spend. Documented hard returns come from replacing external spend, not from revenue.
insights.detail: a16z's January 2026 survey gives the distribution: 19% below break-even, 31% at 1x, 29% at 1.5x, 12% at 2x and 9% at 3x or more. Revenue increase is the least-used ROI measure at 26%. McKinsey finds 37% attributing any EBIT impact and Deloitte 20% achieving revenue growth. MIT NANDA's case examples of $2M to $10M a year from eliminating BPO contracts and 30% lower agency spend came without material internal headcount cuts. AIM's providers confirm from the supply side that outcome-linked pricing stays rare because outcomes are hard to evidence. Enterprises are investing on productivity belief while the measurement discipline catches up.

insights.title: Productivity gains are large on structured work, near zero on judgment work, small in aggregate so far
insights.summary: Controlled studies show gains of 14% to 55% for support agents, developers, marketers and accountants, but no gain for engineers learning new tools and a 19% slowdown for experienced open-source developers that a later replication did not reproduce. Firm-level effects are small so far and the national evidence is early and inconclusive.
insights.detail: Stanford's compilation lists the studies: support agents resolved 14% to 15% more issues per hour, developers with Copilot raised pull requests 26%, marketing teams produced 50% more, accountants 55% more, while experienced developers on familiar codebases were slower and perceived more help than they got. At the macro level, 12,000 European firms show a 4% productivity gain from adoption, a 6,000-executive survey finds minimal realised productivity, and the OECD projects 0.2 to 1.3 points of annual productivity growth over ten years. The Index relays Brynjolfsson's J-curve explanation: firms absorb adoption costs before the larger gains show, and it notes that training strengthens the firm-level gain. That fits the pilot-to-production gap and the workflow-redesign findings elsewhere in this project and gives the site a defensible range to quote.

insights.title: Consumers adopted generative AI faster than any prior technology and capture more value than producers earn
insights.summary: Generative AI reached about 53% of US adults within three years, against 69% for the PC after two decades, and US consumer surplus is estimated at $172B a year. Diffusion tracks national income, with the UAE and Singapore ahead of their income and the US 24th.
insights.detail: Stanford's compilation of Bick and colleagues' adoption tracker and Brynjolfsson's choice experiments shows users rising from 95 million to 115 million US adults and surplus per user from $98 to $125 in a year, with usage frequency the strongest predictor. Microsoft's telemetry, compiled in the Index, puts working-age diffusion at 64% in the UAE, 61% in Singapore, 44% in France, 39% in the UK and 28% in the US and Germany. The consumer numbers are the backdrop to the enterprise activation gap: people already use these tools heavily in private, which is why sanctioned tools are judged against them.

insights.title: Capital into AI companies runs an order of magnitude ahead of enterprise spend on AI, most of all in agents
insights.summary: Corporate investment into AI companies reached about $582B in 2025 against about $37B of enterprise generative AI purchases. Investors put about $8B into agent-focused companies while agent platforms earned about $750M from enterprises.
insights.detail: Quid data compiled by Stanford show private AI investment of $345B and total corporate investment of $582B in 2025, with $143B in infrastructure, models and research alone. Menlo's enterprise spend of $37B is a different measure, purchases rather than capital, but the ratio shows how far ahead of demand the supply side is being funded. In agents the gap is widest: $8.0B invested versus $750M of enterprise agent-platform spend, a ratio above ten to one, while copilots earned $7.2B. Frontier labs illustrate the same pattern: OpenAI's compute spend reached an estimated $16.3B in 2025 against annualised revenue near $25B. The comparison does not show a bubble by itself, but it locates where one would appear first.

insights.title: Model vendor share is shifting toward the newest models and away from open weights
insights.summary: Three quarters of Anthropic's enterprise customers run its latest models in production against under half of OpenAI's, open-weight models fell to about 11% of enterprise usage, and preference swung to closed models with four in five hosting directly with a lab.
insights.detail: a16z finds 75% of Anthropic customers and 76% of Google customers on the most capable model tier in production versus 46% for OpenAI, whose customers often stay on older models that were adopted early and still work. Menlo tracks open-source share falling from 19% to 11% in a year, with Meta's Llama stagnant and Chinese open models at about 1% of enterprise usage despite rapid uptake among startups. a16z's respondents now lean closed (36%) over open (30%), citing pace of quality improvement, thin internal talent and data security, and 81% host directly with a lab, up from about 42% in March 2024. Both firms are investors in the labs they rank, so the shares are estimates with a conflict of interest, but the direction is the same in both.

insights.title: How to read the ten web-era sources: dates, samples and sponsors
insights.summary: The new sources span July 2025 to August 2026, from 100 to 20,000 respondents, and include two venture firms with stakes in the model vendors they rank, three consultancies that sell AI transformation, one software vendor, one MIT research project and one academic compilation.
insights.detail: Fieldwork order matters when sources disagree: NANDA (Jan to Jun 2025), Deloitte (Aug to Sep 2025), Menlo (Nov 2025), BCG (late 2025, published Jan 2026), a16z (Jan 2026), Microsoft (Feb to Apr 2026), KPMG and McKinsey (May to Jun 2026). Samples range from a16z's 100 Global 2000 executives and KPMG's 204 US leaders to Deloitte's 3,235, BCG's 2,360 and Microsoft's 20,000 AI users, and only McKinsey has a large sub-$1B, GDP-weighted global sample. Deloitte, Microsoft and Menlo survey only organisations or people already using AI, which raises every adoption figure. Menlo invests in Anthropic and a16z in OpenAI; BCG, Deloitte, KPMG and McKinsey sell AI consulting; Microsoft sells Copilot; NANDA promotes its own agent protocols; Stanford compiles others' data with a year's lag. IDC's FutureScape page is forecasts only. The site labels each finding's source and population so readers can weigh it.

insights.title: Outlook: spending keeps growing through 2026, at a slower rate than the January surveys expected
insights.summary: Where sources agree: every one of them shows AI budgets rising and no source shows retreat. Where they differ: early-2026 surveys expected a doubling; mid-2026 surveys show steady growth with most increases under 30%.
insights.detail: BCG's CEOs expected AI investment to double as a share of revenue in 2026 and 94% would keep investing even without a 2026 payoff. a16z's CIOs projected 65% growth in LLM spend after actual 2025 spend beat their own forecast by more than half. Menlo measured 3.2x market growth in 2025. The two surveys fielded in May and June 2026 are softer: McKinsey finds 61% increasing but only 8% by 30% or more, and KPMG's projected 12-month spend is flat at about $200M after doubling over the prior year. The difference is timing, not contradiction. Our expectation for the next twelve months is continued growth in the 10% to 30% band for most organisations, with the doubling concentrated in the leading minority, and with 2027 editions of BCG and a16z the test.

insights.title: Outlook: agents become a majority practice on paper by 2027, while governed agentic systems stay a minority
insights.summary: Where sources agree: every survey expects agent use to rise sharply and orchestration is where budgets and vendors are moving. Where they differ: self-reported adoption already reaches half; architectural and stage-based measures sit at 13% to 22% and moved little in the first half of 2026.
insights.detail: Deloitte's respondents expect at-least-moderate agent use to reach 74% within two years and IDC forecasts half of enterprises by 2027, which the self-reports from KPMG (53% deployed) already claim. Menlo's 16% true agents, a16z's 13% agentic workflow automation, McKinsey's 22% scaling below $1B revenue and Microsoft's 25% to 29% of advanced users with documented agent workflows describe the real base. Expect the self-reported numbers to cross a majority by 2027 as vendors relabel workflows as agents, while the share of organisations running governed, repeatable, multi-step agent processes climbs more slowly from roughly one in five, led by large firms where McKinsey already finds 40%. KPMG's doubling of orchestration in one quarter is the leading indicator to watch, together with agent-action risk controls in McKinsey's next edition.

insights.title: Outlook: the binding constraint has moved from technology to the organisation; the leading group stays small
insights.summary: Where sources agree: skills, workflow redesign, manager practice and incentives explain who captures value; the practice-defined leading group is 15% to 20% in every source that measures it. Where they differ: only on how the bar is set, from 6% to 34%.
insights.detail: AIM's providers, Deloitte's leaders, Microsoft's AI users, BCG's CEOs and McKinsey's high performers all locate the constraint in adoption, redesign and organisational conditions rather than in models or tools. Microsoft's factor analysis attributes twice as much reported impact to organisational conditions as to individual effort; McKinsey's high performers redesign workflows at three times the rate of others; Deloitte finds 84% have not redesigned jobs. The leading share clusters at 15% (BCG), 16% to 19% (Microsoft) and 20% (IDC) when defined by practice. Our expectation is that this share grows slowly, because the practices involved (workflow redesign, decision rights, incentive changes) take years, and that the gap between leaders and the rest widens in outcomes before it narrows in adoption, which is what IDC's tier data already show.

insights.title: Outlook: enterprise financial proof arrives later than the productivity gains, if the J-curve holds
insights.summary: Where sources agree: personal productivity gains are broad and efficiency is largely captured; attributable EBIT and revenue impact is rare and flat. Where they differ: executives expect ROI in 2026; measured evidence suggests a lag of years at the organisation level.
insights.detail: McKinsey's 80% personal productivity against 37% EBIT attribution and 6% high performers, Deloitte's 66% efficiency against 20% revenue, and a16z's half at break-even or worse describe the same state from three angles. BCG's CEOs expect agents to unlock measurable ROI during 2026. The AI Index's evidence table supplies the reason for caution: micro gains of 14% to 55% on structured work coexist with a 4% firm-level effect in Europe and negligible aggregate productivity contribution so far. The productivity J-curve frames the expectation: returns follow complementary investment in workflows, data and skills, which the leading minority is making now. The indicators to watch are EBIT attribution and ROI multiples in the 2027 editions of McKinsey and a16z, and whether Deloitte's revenue-achieved share moves off 20%.

insights.title: Outlook: cost discipline becomes a standard practice as usage volume outruns falling unit prices
insights.summary: Where sources agree: token and operating costs are now a constraint for a fifth of organisations, visibility is poor, and volume growth outpaces price declines. No source disagrees; the buyer surveys differ only in how much weight cost gets relative to data and skills.
insights.detail: McKinsey's 20% limiting AI use on cost and 18% of high performers constrained on coding agents, KPMG's 26% with full cost visibility and 36% with token budgets, AIM's warning about costs scaling from proof of concept to production, and the Jevons framing in Menlo and McKinsey all point the same way. IDC's buyers rank LLM cost only sixth of seven barriers, which shows cost is not yet the top concern but is rising as agents scale. Our expectation is that token budgets, cost review at approval, routing to cheaper models and cost literacy become table stakes within a year, as FinOps did for cloud, and that usage-based incentives such as token-maxxing fade in favour of outcome measures. Vendors that sell cost controls, which AIM already finds among its Leaders, benefit.

insights.title: Outlook: buy the applications and platforms, build the long tail with coding agents
insights.summary: Where sources agree: packaged applications and trusted incumbents win the enterprise seat, and bought solutions reach production faster than internal builds. Where they differ: McKinsey's mid-2026 data show coding agents already displacing a third of organisations' software purchases.
insights.detail: Menlo, a16z, NANDA, AIM and Deloitte converge on buying over building for applications, with trust and integration favouring incumbents and speed favouring AI-native startups. McKinsey's 32% declining a purchase in favour of building with coding agents, rising to about half of high performers, points to a bifurcation rather than a reversal: enterprises buy horizontal copilots, agent platforms and vertical products, and build the features, integrations and internal tools they once bought as add-ons. Our expectation is a vendor landscape with incumbents holding the broad licence, a smaller set of AI-native specialists owning high-token workloads such as coding and clinical documentation, and a thinning long tail of point solutions. For the services market AIM describes, this raises the premium on production evidence and orchestration platforms and lowers it on bespoke builds.

insights.title: Outlook: workforce effects arrive at about half the pace executives expect, and hit entry-level roles first
insights.summary: Where sources agree: cuts are expected to concentrate in service operations, supply chain and administrative work, and human oversight demand rises before headcount falls. Where they differ: executive expectations (a third to 82% of firms) far exceed realised effects (14% reported cuts; limited layoffs in NANDA's sample).
insights.detail: McKinsey's before-and-after check shows expected cuts of 32% against 14% reported, with expectations rising to 39% anyway. Deloitte and BCG expect far more automation than that, while NANDA documents limited, selective cuts in already-disrupted sectors and mostly outsourced roles. The AI Index shows where the cost is landing first: employment of 22-to-25-year-olds fell close to 20% in software development and about 16% relative in the most exposed occupations. KPMG's rising workload-driven resistance and McKinsey's strain below executive level show the pressure inside firms. Our expectation for the next two years is realised headcount effects at roughly half of stated expectations, concentrated in support, admin and junior technical roles, with the offset in oversight, evaluation and agent-operations roles that Lightcast data already show employers hiring for.

insights.title: Outlook: governance closes the gap at the leaders first, while sovereignty and public trust shape the rest
insights.summary: Where sources agree: agent governance lags deployment, privacy and security top every concern list, and human-in-the-loop is the default control. Where they differ: a16z's US and UK enterprises are moving toward direct hosting with frontier labs while Deloitte's global sample is moving toward local vendors and data residency.
insights.detail: Deloitte's 21% with mature agent governance, KPMG's output-level human review at 52%, McKinsey's 33% mitigating unauthorised agent action (45% among high performers) and BCG's expectation that agent autonomy triples describe a gap that the leading minority is closing first. Sovereignty pulls in a different direction by geography: 83% of Deloitte's respondents treat data residency as important and 77% weigh country of origin, while 81% of a16z's Global 2000 firms host directly with a lab. The AI Index adds that publics trust the EU more than the US or China to regulate AI and that US trust in its own regulator is lowest. Our expectation is regulation-driven divergence: audit trails, decision rights and agent identity become standard at large firms within two years; European and Gulf buyers favour local hosting and sovereign stacks; US buyers consolidate on frontier labs; and public trust remains a brake on consumer-facing deployment in the West.

insights.title: Outlook: physical AI grows in controlled environments and in Asia; the two-year jump to 80% is an expectation
insights.summary: Where sources agree: physical AI is already present at most adopters, Asia leads, and factories and warehouses move first. Where they differ: Deloitte's respondents expect 80% adoption within two years, while robot shipment data were flat in 2024 with US installations down 9%.
insights.detail: Deloitte finds 58% of AI-using companies with at least limited physical AI use and 18% at a moderate level, with cost the top barrier because retrofits, integration and maintenance dwarf the software. The IFR data compiled by Stanford show 542,000 industrial robots installed in 2024, up 0.2%, with China at 54% of the world, collaborative robots at 13.6% of installations, and service robots for logistics growing. Microsoft's telemetry shows manufacturing running the deepest agent estates among few adopting firms, which suggests in-house builds on platforms rather than bought vertical products, consistent with Menlo's tiny manufacturing vertical market. Our expectation is steady expansion of intelligent monitoring, cobots and digital twins in controlled settings, led by Asia Pacific, and slower progress in open environments where safety regulation and liability apply.

insights.title: Outlook: where the sources disagree, and why
insights.summary: Five disagreements run through the twelve sources: which model vendor leads, whether company size matters, how many pilots fail, how fast spend grows, and how many jobs go. In each case the sources measure different things or different populations, and the notes record the reconciliation.
insights.detail: Vendor leadership: Menlo (Anthropic, API usage, broad US sample, Anthropic investor) versus a16z (OpenAI, production footprint and wallet share among Global 2000 firms, OpenAI investor); both agree on direction. Size: McKinsey and the AI Index show large firms far ahead on deployment stage; IDC and AIM show maturity and delivery challenges flat by size; breadth of deployment is not maturity of practice. Failure: NANDA's 5% success is custom tools judged on sustained P&L within six months; AIM's 25% to 45% is vendor POCs; Menlo's 47% is bought solutions; Deloitte's 25% is firms past a production threshold. Spend: January surveys expected doubling, May and June surveys show moderation. Jobs: expectations of a third to four fifths of firms against 14% reported cuts and NANDA's limited layoffs. The site presents each pair with its definitions rather than picking a side, because the disagreement itself is the finding readers need.

insights.title: Outlook: eight indicators to watch in the 2027 editions
insights.summary: The next round of these reports will show whether the 2026 expectations held. The notes name the specific numbers to compare.
insights.detail: One: Deloitte's share of firms with 40% or more of experiments in production, expected to rise from 25% to 54%. Two: McKinsey's EBIT attribution (37%) and high-performer share (6%), both flat for two years. Three: a16z's ROI distribution, currently half at break-even or worse, and its wallet-share trend for Anthropic, Google and OpenAI. Four: KPMG's agent deployment rate (53%) and orchestration share (18%), the earliest read on whether the plateau persists. Five: McKinsey's reported versus expected headcount change, currently 14% against 39%. Six: the share of organisations with mature agent governance (Deloitte 21%) and mitigating unauthorised agent action (McKinsey 33%). Seven: BCG's investment as a share of revenue, expected to reach 1.7%. Eight: Menlo's agent-platform spend against copilots, currently $750M against $7.2B, and Quid's agent investment against it. Movement on these eight will tell readers whether 2026 was the year agents moved from pilots to production or the year expectations were reset.
